Hi Andreia, it's David again. Your pitch went very well, so now they want you on a panel next month, with a Q and A session after it. Here is my advice for the questions. First, never bluff. If you do not know the answer, say so, and promise to get back to them by email. People respect that. Second, use careful language. Instead of saying robotic surgery is always better, say it tends to be better for complex cases, or the evidence suggests it. Third, if a question is beyond the scope of your talk, say it is a fair question, and send it to the right person. And finally, when someone is skeptical, do not get defensive. Thank them, take a breath, and answer the part you can answer. You will be fine.

That is a fair question, thank you. You asked if our training program is really worth the cost. I would say that it is, but let me be careful with the numbers. Off the top of my head, the program cost about two hundred thousand reais in the first year. The evidence suggests that trained teams tend to have shorter surgeries and fewer complications, so the program is likely to pay for itself in about two years. However, it seems that the savings depend on the number of surgeries, and I do not have the exact data for every hospital here. Let me check with our finance team and get back to you by Friday.

This is how Andreia answers a tough question. First, she thanks the person and says it is a fair question. Then she repeats the question in her own words. Next, she gives a careful answer with hedging, like I would say that. After that, she admits what she does not know, without bluffing. Finally, she promises to check and get back to the person.
